Source: http://www.norml.org

Posted March 15, 2000
MEMORANDUM

FROM: Tom Dean, Esq.
Litigation Director
NORML Foundation

RE: Legal issues in connection with the use and distribution of Medical Marijuana in the District of Columbia

Initiative 59, the " Legalization of Marijuana for Medical Treatment Initiative of 1998 " was prevented from becoming law, at least temporarily, by the Congress by amendment to the appropriations bill. I-59 provided that qualifying individuals, their " primary care givers ", and non profit organizations organized pursuant to I-59 were to be exempt from prosecution under the Districts Controlled Substance Act (DC Code 33-501, et sec.).
Qualifying individuals would have been able to cultivate and purchase and use marijuana for medical use. Primary care givers and qualifying organizations would have been able to cultivate, purchase and distribute marijuana to qualifying individuals.

Medical marijuana initiatives, like I-59, provide for an exemption to prosecution for the use of medical marijuana. Because I-59 was blocked by Congress, no such exemption is currently available in the District. However, D.C. and some other states that have not passed initiatives, have recognized a medical necessity defense that can be used at trial, after one has been charged with a criminal offense. Medical necessity is a criminal defense that has been developed by the courts in the United States and elsewhere.

In United States v. Randall, 104 Daily Wash. L. Rep. 2249 (D.C. Super. Ct. Nov. 24, 1976), the Superior Court of the District of Columbia extended the necessity defense to a defendant who illegally grew and used marijuana to alleviate the symptoms of glaucoma. The court in Randall interpreted the medical necessity doctrine to permit an individual threatened by disease and eventual loss of health to escape criminal liability for growing and using marijuana where the use was designed to alleviate the disease's threat to his
well-being. The court characterized actions dictated by necessity as conscious and rational acts guided, not by free will, but by the absence of an acceptable alternative to breaking the law.


In considering whether the evil avoided by Randall's action was less than the evil inherent in the offense charged, the court balanced defendant's interests and those of the Government. It found the defendant's wish to preserve his eyesight obvious. In assessing the Government's interests, the court noted that the danger of marijuana smoking was uncertain. The court decided that Randall's legitimate health care issues outweighed any " slight, speculative and undemonstrable " social harm that his use of marijuana might
cause. Id. At 2253.

It is unclear whether federal law allows for a medical marijuana defense, although the Ninth Circuit Federal Court of Appeals has ruled that it does.

In United States v. OCBC, decided in September, 1999, the court held that federal law allows patients and buyers clubs to who cultivate and distribute marijuana to present a medical marijuana defense at trial. This decision was affirmed again by the Ninth Circuit in United States v. B.E. Smith, decided earlier this year.

The Ninth Circuit decision is much more explicit and comprehensive than the Randall decision, so it should be used as a model for defining medical necessity. The ninth Circuit held that an organization may distribute and a person may use marijuana medically where:

1. The patient suffers from a serious medical condition;

2. If the patient does not have access to cannabis, the patient will suffer imminent harm;

3. Cannabis is necessary for the treatment of the patient's medical condition or cannabis will alleviate the medical condition or symptoms associated with it;

4. There is no legal alternative to cannabis for the effective treatment of the patient's medical condition because the patient has tried other legal alternatives to cannabis and has found them ineffective in treating the patient's condition or has found that such alternatives result in intolerable side effects.

Again, where a patient satisfies these conditions, he or she is not immune from being charged with a criminal offense. Rather, if charged, a person or organization can defend against the charges by arguing that he or she used marijuana out of a medical necessity. Such a defense is authorized by Randall in D.C. Courts and by OCBC and Smith in federal courts within the Ninth Circuit. However, the Ninth Circuit's jurisdiction extends only to
several western states. To date, the D.C. Circuit Federal Court of Appeals has not taken up the issue, so it is uncertain whether it would follow the Ninth Circuit's decision in OCBC and B.E. Smith.

See
Federal Jury Convicts Vietnam Veteran Of Growing Medical Marijuana
After Judge Blocks Medical Defense; Woody Harrelson Rebukes Judge. -- 2 Articles

As a practical matter, the Federal Government does not prosecute personal use offenses. Those cases are left to the D.C. Courts where they are prosecuted as misdemeanors. However, the Federal Government has indicated its willingness to prosecute buyers clubs under federal law, outside the Ninth Circuit, despite the club's compliance with the guidelines set forth in the OCBC case.

In order for D.C. residents to protect themselves as much as possible from prosecution and conviction for using or distributing medical marijuana, they should be certain that they have complied with the above guidelines.
